course: Small Kiosk and Tuck Shop Business

lessons.title: Calculating Cost of Goods Sold
lessons.body:
To make a profit, you must first know exactly what each item costs you. Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) is the total cost of the products you sell. For a kiosk, this includes the purchase price of goods, transport to bring them to your stall, and any packaging you use. For example, if you buy a crate of 24 bottles of soda for 2400 KES, each bottle costs 100 KES. If you pay 100 KES for transport, add that to the total cost: 2400 + 100 = 2500 KES. Now each bottle costs 2500 / 24 = about 104 KES. Always calculate COGS per unit so you know your break-even price.

Keep a simple notebook or use a free app like Excel or Google Sheets on your phone. Record every purchase: date, item, quantity, unit cost, and total cost. At the end of each day, calculate your COGS by adding up the cost of all items sold. For instance, if you sold 10 sodas, 5 packets of biscuits, and 20 sweets, you need the cost per unit for each. If biscuits cost 50 KES per packet and sweets cost 5 KES each, your COGS for the day is (10 x 104) + (5 x 50) + (20 x 5) = 1040 + 250 + 100 = 1390 KES. Subtract this from your total sales to get your gross profit.

Remember to include hidden costs like electricity for a fridge, airtime for mobile money, or spoilage. If milk expires, that cost must be spread over the remaining units. For example, if you buy 20 litres of milk at 60 KES each and 2 litres spoil, your effective cost per litre becomes (20 x 60) / 18 = 66.67 KES. Always round up to the nearest shilling to stay safe. Review your COGS weekly to spot price changes from suppliers. If the price of cooking oil rises, adjust your selling price quickly. Without accurate COGS, you might think you are making profit when you are actually losing money. So, start today: list your top 10 products, calculate their unit costs, and write them on a card you keep at your stall.

lessons.title: Setting Profit Margins and Markups
lessons.body:
Profit margin and markup are two ways to set your selling price. Markup is the amount you add to the cost price to get the selling price. Profit margin is the percentage of the selling price that is profit. For example, if an item costs 100 KES and you sell it for 150 KES, your markup is 50 KES (50% of cost). Your profit margin is 50/150 = 33.3%. Many kiosk owners use a simple rule: double the cost price (100% markup) for fast-moving items like sweets, and add 20-30% for staples like bread or milk. But be careful: high markup may scare customers away, while low markup may not cover your expenses.

To set a markup, first know your COGS per unit. Then decide on a target profit margin based on your total monthly expenses. Suppose your rent, transport, and airtime cost 10,000 KES per month. If you expect to sell 500 items, you need 20 KES profit per item just to cover these costs. So if an item costs 80 KES, you must sell it for at least 100 KES. That is a 25% markup. For luxury or impulse items like chocolate, you can charge 50-100% markup because customers are less price-sensitive. For competitive items like maize flour, keep markup low (10-15%) to attract customers.

Use a simple formula: Selling Price = Cost Price + (Cost Price x Markup Percentage). For a 40% markup on a 50 KES item: 50 + (50 x 0.4) = 70 KES. Always round to a friendly number like 70 or 75. Review your markups every month. If a supplier increases prices, recalculate. If you sell in bulk, you can lower markup per unit but earn more total profit. For example, selling a single sweet at 2 KES with 100% markup gives 1 KES profit. Selling a pack of 10 sweets for 15 KES (cost 10 KES) gives 5 KES profit, but the markup is only 50%. The key is to balance volume and margin. Track your best-selling items and adjust markups to maximise total profit, not just per-unit profit.

lessons.title: Competitive Pricing Techniques
lessons.body:
In a competitive market, your prices must attract customers while covering costs. Start by checking what nearby kiosks and shops charge for the same items. Walk around your area and note prices for your top 10 products. If a competitor sells a 500ml soda for 50 KES, you can price yours at 50 KES to match, or 48 KES to undercut slightly. But never go below your COGS. If your cost is 45 KES, selling at 48 KES gives only 3 KES profitâtoo low unless you sell huge volumes. Instead, focus on differentiation: offer cold drinks when others sell warm ones, or open earlier when others are closed.

Use a strategy called 'loss leader': price a few popular items very low, even at break-even, to draw customers. Once they come for the cheap bread, they may buy other items with higher margins. For example, sell a loaf of bread at 55 KES when competitors sell at 60 KES. You make only 5 KES on bread, but customers also buy milk, sugar, and airtime. Another technique is bundle pricing: sell a packet of biscuits and a soda together for 80 KES instead of 85 KES separately. This increases total sales and clears slow-moving stock.

Monitor competitors weekly. If they lower prices, don't panic. First, check if you can negotiate lower prices from your supplier. Buy in larger quantities to get discounts. If not, emphasise value: clean stall, friendly service, or credit for trusted customers. In many African markets, customers value relationships over a few shillings. You can also offer a loyalty card: buy 10 sodas, get one free. This locks in customers without lowering your regular price. Remember, competing only on price is a race to the bottom. Compete on convenience, quality, and trust. Keep a small notebook of competitor prices and your own, and review it every two weeks.

lessons.title: Psychological Pricing Tactics
lessons.body:
Psychological pricing uses human psychology to make prices feel more attractive. The most common tactic is charm pricing: set prices just below a round number, like 99 KES instead of 100 KES, or 49 KES instead of 50 KES. Customers perceive 99 as significantly cheaper than 100, even though it's only 1 shilling less. In many African markets, prices like 95, 98, or 99 work well. For very small items, like sweets, you can use 5 KES, 10 KES, but for items above 20 KES, charm pricing is effective. For example, a packet of tea that costs you 70 KES can be sold at 99 KES instead of 100 KESâit feels like a bargain.

Another tactic is anchoring: place a higher-priced item next to a lower-priced one to make the lower price seem like a great deal. For instance, display a large bag of rice for 500 KES next to a smaller bag for 250 KES. The 250 KES bag looks affordable. You can also use 'buy one get one free' or '3 for 100 KES' to encourage bulk purchases. For example, if a single soap costs 40 KES, offer 3 for 100 KES (33.33 KES each). Customers feel they are saving, and you sell more units. But ensure the bundle price still covers your costs and gives a profit.

Use round prices for premium items. A fancy chocolate bar at 100 KES feels more luxurious than 99 KES. For everyday items, use charm pricing. Also, consider the 'rule of 100': for items under 100 KES, a percentage discount (e.g., 20% off) sounds better; for items over 100 KES, a shilling discount (e.g., 50 KES off) sounds better. For example, a 200 KES item with '50 KES off' is more appealing than '25% off'. Finally, always display prices clearly. Handwritten signs with big numbers work well. Avoid too many decimalsâround to the nearest shilling. Test different prices on a few items and see what sells best. Small changes can increase your profit without losing customers.

lessons.title: Discounts and Promotions Without Losing Profit
lessons.body:
Discounts and promotions can boost sales, but they can also destroy your profit if not planned. The golden rule: never discount below your COGS plus a minimum profit. Before offering any discount, calculate your break-even price. For example, if an item costs 80 KES, and you need at least 10 KES profit per unit to cover overheads, your minimum selling price is 90 KES. So a discount from 120 KES to 100 KES is safe, but to 85 KES is not. Use discounts to clear slow-moving stock or attract new customers, not on your best-sellers that already sell well.

Common promotions include 'buy 2 get 1 free', '10% off on weekends', or 'free airtime with purchase of 500 KES'. For 'buy 2 get 1 free', the effective price per unit drops. If a soda costs 50 KES, selling 3 for 100 KES means each is 33.33 KES. If your COGS is 40 KES, you lose money. So only run this if your COGS is below 33 KES. Instead, try 'buy 3 get a small sweet free'âthe sweet costs you 2 KES, but you sell 3 sodas at full price. That's a better promotion. Another idea: offer a discount only on a bundle. For example, a packet of maize flour and cooking oil together for 200 KES instead of 220 KES separately. Your total cost might be 170 KES, so you still make 30 KES profit.

Time-limited promotions create urgency. 'Today only: 10% off all biscuits' can bring in customers who then buy other items. But avoid daily discountsâcustomers will wait for them. Use promotions for special events like holidays or back-to-school. Track the results: did sales increase enough to offset the lower price? If you sold 20 units at 100 KES (profit 20 KES each = 400 KES) versus 30 units at 90 KES (profit 10 KES each = 300 KES), you made less profit despite more sales. So always calculate. Keep a simple record of promotion sales and profits. If a promotion doesn't increase total profit, stop it. Remember, the goal is profit, not just revenue.

lessons.title: Adjusting Prices Based on Demand
lessons.body:
Demand for products changes based on time, weather, and events. Adjusting prices based on demand can increase your profit. For example, on a hot day, cold drinks are in high demand. You can charge 10-20% more for a cold soda than on a cool day. If a 500ml soda normally sells for 50 KES, on a hot day you can sell it for 60 KES. Customers are willing to pay for relief from the heat. Similarly, during Ramadan or Christmas, demand for certain foods like dates or biscuits rises. You can increase prices slightly, but be careful not to exploit customersâthey may resent it and go elsewhere.

Another demand factor is time of day. In the morning, people rush to work and buy breakfast items like bread and tea. You can charge a premium for convenience. In the evening, demand for snacks and airtime increases. If you notice a product selling out quickly, you can raise its price. But test small increases: raise by 5 KES and see if sales hold. If sales drop too much, revert. Use a simple demand diary: note daily sales for each product and weather conditions. After a month, you'll see patterns. For example, you might find that on rainy days, umbrellas and hot tea sell more, so you can stock up and price slightly higher.

Also, consider seasonal demand. During school holidays, more children buy sweets and snacks. You can create small 'holiday packs' at a higher price. During planting season, farmers may have less cash, so demand for cheap items rises. You can lower prices on staples to keep volume, but maintain prices on treats. Always communicate price changes politely: 'Due to high demand, cold drinks are 60 KES today.' Most customers understand. Never change prices too oftenâit confuses customers. Adjust based on clear patterns, not guesses. Keep your cost in mind: even with high demand, never sell below cost. The goal is to maximise profit when demand is high, and maintain sales when demand is low.

quiz.q: What does COGS stand for?
quiz.explanation: COGS is the total cost of the products you sell, including purchase price and transport.

quiz.q: If you buy 12 bottles of soda for 600 KES and pay 50 KES transport, what is the cost per bottle?
quiz.explanation: Total cost = 600 + 50 = 650 KES; 650 / 12 = 54.17 KES per bottle.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a hidden cost that should be included in COGS?
quiz.explanation: Electricity for a fridge is a direct cost of storing goods for sale, so it is part of COGS.

quiz.q: If 2 litres of milk spoil out of 20 litres bought at 60 KES each, what is the effective cost per litre?
quiz.explanation: Total cost = 20 x 60 = 1200 KES; usable litres = 18; 1200 / 18 = 66.67 KES.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate COGS per unit?
options: A) To know your break-even price
D) To decide on staff wages
quiz.explanation: Knowing COGS per unit helps you set a selling price that covers costs and yields profit.

quiz.q: What is markup?
options: A) The percentage of selling price that is profit
B) The amount added to cost price to get selling price
C) The discount given to customers
quiz.explanation: Markup is the amount added to the cost price to determine the selling price.

quiz.q: If an item costs 100 KES and sells for 150 KES, what is the profit margin?
quiz.explanation: Profit margin = (selling price - cost) / selling price = 50/150 = 33.3%.

quiz.q: Which formula correctly calculates selling price with markup?
options: A) Selling Price = Cost Price - Markup
B) Selling Price = Cost Price + (Cost Price x Markup %)
C) Selling Price = Cost Price / Markup %
D) Selling Price = Markup % / Cost Price
quiz.explanation: Markup is a percentage of cost, so you add it to cost price to get selling price.

quiz.q: If your monthly overheads are 10,000 KES and you expect to sell 500 items, what is the minimum profit per item to cover overheads?
quiz.explanation: 10,000 / 500 = 20 KES profit per item needed just to cover overheads.

quiz.q: For a 40% markup on a 50 KES item, what is the selling price?
What is a loss leader?
options: A) A product sold at a very low price to attract customers
B) A product that always makes a loss
C) A product with high profit margin
D) A product that is given free
quiz.explanation: A loss leader is priced low (even at break-even) to draw customers who then buy other profitable items.

quiz.q: Which of these is a competitive pricing technique?
options: C) Charging the highest price possible
quiz.explanation: Bundling products (e.g., biscuits and soda together) is a competitive pricing technique to increase sales.

quiz.q: If a competitor sells a soda for 50 KES and your cost is 45 KES, what is a safe competitive price?
quiz.explanation: 48 KES is above cost (45 KES) and slightly below competitor, giving a small profit while attracting customers.

quiz.q: What is a loyalty card?
options: A) A card that gives discounts to all customers
B) A card that rewards repeat customers after a certain number of purchases
C) A card for paying with credit
quiz.explanation: A loyalty card rewards repeat customers, e.g., buy 10 sodas get one free, without lowering regular prices.

quiz.q: Why is competing only on price a 'race to the bottom'?
options: A) Because it always increases profit
B) Because it can lead to prices below cost and no profit
C) Because customers prefer high prices
quiz.explanation: If everyone lowers prices, eventually prices fall below cost, leaving no profit for anyone.

quiz.q: What is charm pricing?
options: A) Setting prices just below a round number, like 99 instead of 100
B) Setting prices at round numbers
C) Giving free gifts with purchase
D) Charging different prices for different customers
quiz.explanation: Charm pricing uses prices like 99 KES to make customers perceive the price as significantly lower.

quiz.q: Which pricing tactic involves placing a higher-priced item next to a lower-priced one?
quiz.explanation: Anchoring uses a high-priced item to make the lower-priced item seem like a better deal.

quiz.q: For an item under 100 KES, which discount framing is more effective?
quiz.explanation: For items under 100 KES, percentage discounts (e.g., 20% off) sound more appealing than shilling discounts.

quiz.q: What is the 'rule of 100' in psychological pricing?
options: B) For items under 100 KES, use percentage discounts; for over 100 KES, use shilling discounts
C) Never charge more than 100 KES
D) Give 100 KES discount on all items
quiz.explanation: The rule of 100 suggests percentage discounts work better for low-priced items, while shilling discounts work better for high-priced items.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid too many decimals in prices?
options: A) Because customers prefer round numbers
B) Because it confuses customers and slows transactions
quiz.explanation: Decimals like 99.99 can confuse customers and make giving change difficult; rounding to nearest shilling is simpler.

quiz.q: When offering a discount, what is the golden rule?
options: A) Always give at least 50% off
B) Never discount below COGS plus a minimum profit
quiz.explanation: Discounts should never go below your cost plus a minimum profit to cover overheads.

quiz.q: If an item costs 80 KES and you need 10 KES profit per unit, what is the minimum selling price?
quiz.explanation: Minimum selling price = cost + minimum profit = 80 + 10 = 90 KES.

quiz.q: Which promotion is safe if your soda cost is 40 KES?
options: A) Buy 2 get 1 free at 50 KES each
C) Buy 3 get a small sweet free
quiz.explanation: Buy 3 get a sweet free: you sell 3 sodas at full price (profit 10 KES each) and give a sweet costing 2 KES, still profitable.

quiz.q: What should you track when running a promotion?
options: B) Total profit before and after promotion
quiz.explanation: Track total profit to ensure the promotion increased profit, not just sales.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate break-even price before discounting?
options: A) To know the lowest price you can charge without losing money
C) To set the highest price
quiz.explanation: Break-even price is the minimum price that covers all costs; discounting below it means you lose money.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good time to offer a promotion?
options: C) When you have no stock
quiz.explanation: Promotions during special events like holidays or back-to-school can attract more customers and boost sales.

quiz.q: What is demand-based pricing?
options: A) Setting prices based on customer demand
B) Setting prices based on cost only
C) Setting prices based on competitor prices only
quiz.explanation: Demand-based pricing adjusts prices up or down depending on how much customers want the product at a given time.

quiz.q: On a hot day, what can you do with cold drink prices?
options: A) Lower them to attract customers
quiz.explanation: High demand for cold drinks on a hot day allows you to increase prices slightly without losing sales.

quiz.q: How can you identify demand patterns?
options: B) By keeping a daily sales diary with weather notes
quiz.explanation: A daily sales diary recording sales and weather helps you see patterns and adjust prices accordingly.

quiz.q: What should you do if you raise a price by 5 KES and sales drop too much?
options: B) Keep it and accept lower sales
C) Revert to the original price
quiz.explanation: If a price increase causes a large drop in sales, revert to the original price to maintain volume and profit.

quiz.q: Why should you never change prices too often?
options: A) It confuses customers and may drive them away
quiz.explanation: Frequent price changes confuse customers and can erode trust; adjust only based on clear demand patterns.
